newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY-YZERMAN BASKS IN LONG-AWAITED CUP VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY-YZERMAN BASKS IN LONG-AWAITED CUP VICTORY.

text.p: In the end, Detroit Red Wings captain Steve Yzerman was nearly too much of a team player to take the solo Stanley Cup victory lap traditionally awarded the leader of the winning team.

As thousands of fans worked themselves into a deafening frenzy at Joe Louis Arena, Yzerman's teammates had to prod him into hoisting the freshly polished cup and basking in the glory by himself after the Red Wings held off the Philadelphia Flyers 2-1 Saturday to sweep the NHL finals in four games.
"I kind of wanted to do it as a team, but it was kind of neat to do it alone as well," Yzerman said.
The victory was a long time in coming -- not just for the Red Wings -- who had not won the Cup since 1955 -- but for Yzerman.
The heart and soul of the Red Wings and one of the league's elite players for 14 years, Yzerman has been playing his heart out for Detroit since his NHL career began in 1983.
Named the team's captain in 1986 at just 21 years of age, his wait for a Stanley Cup victory has been agonizingly long.

His team was favoured to win the Cup in 1994, 1995 and 1996, but each year ended in bitter disappointment -- first a stunning first-round upset by the upstart San Jose Sharks, then a sweep out of the finals at the hands of the underdog New Jersey Devils.

Last year was the unkindest cut of all, when Detroit posted an NHL regular-season record 62 victories only to lose in the semifinals in six games to Colorado, leaving Yzerman shaken and wondering if he would ever see his name on the Stanley Cup.
On Saturday, the quiet, reserved Wings captain was almost at a loss as to how to put his feelings into words.
"I don't know how to describe how I feel. I wish -- I'm glad the game is over, but I wish it never would have ended," he said.
"The things you go through in your whole career, you get some heartbreaks, some good times, nothing compares to this," he said. "I wish every player got an opportunity to go through this just once."

As he has throughout the series with Philadelphia, Yzerman was all over the ice Saturday, penetrating the Flyers' shaky defence, and using his own body to block shots before they could get to Red Wings goalie Mike Vernon.

Yzerman did not have a goal Saturday after scoring in each of the first three games of the finals. Although he did get an assist for starting the play that sent Darren McCarty streaking alone into the Flyers' zone to score the goal that turned out to be the game winner in the second period.
But for his legions of fans in Detroit, it was enough to see Yzerman holding the cup aloft after so many years.
Patty Segvich, wearing a red jersey with Yzerman's number 19, said the sole reason she attended Saturday was the chance to see the man known locally as "Stevie" hold the cup aloft.
"There are so many mediocre players who have rings and have gotten to hold the Cup," she said. "I want to see Stevie hold it up."
And hold it up he did, to the delight of his adoring fans.
"The city has really supported our team and stuck behind me," Yzerman said. "We've done some good things but we've always come up short. But we stuck together.
"I just love it here. This is my home and I'm staying here forever."
And what ever he does in the rest of his Hall of Fame career, his name will be on the Stanley Cup forever.
